entry.title: Seven hundred students across three subjects say what escape rooms actually taught them
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Auckland and Bond University surveyed students and educators about escape room games used in three distinct degree programmes at one large university, and received 708 student responses and eight educator responses. The quantitative answers were analysed descriptively and the written answers by thematic analysis. Students and educators in medical sciences, biological sciences and education all reported rich and many-sided learning, and the authors found that escape rooms promoted similar transferable skills and motivations whatever the disciplinary context. Their recommendation is to use escape rooms sparingly.

Why it matters here: It gives the Wits study a survey design and a sample size to aim at, and its finding that the gains hold across very different disciplines is an argument for trying an escape room in metallurgy at all. The advice to use them sparingly is a useful check on how often a gamified activity should appear in one course.

Kam, M., Clune, M., Jowsey, T. and Singleton, R., Higher Education Research and Development, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND

entry.title: A mining and metallurgy school built its own simulation game for its own exploration course
entry.summary:
Three staff at the School of Mining and Metallurgical Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens used a design-based research approach to build and evaluate an educational simulation game for probabilistic and spatial reasoning in mineral exploration. The application generates random scenarios in which players direct exploration decisions and end by estimating ore reserves. The game has been adopted as a teaching tool in the course Introduction to Mineral Exploration at the school, and the paper reports game analytics together with a qualitative evaluation drawn from three workshops at higher education institutions in Greece.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published parallel to the Wits study: a mining and metallurgical engineering school designing a game for its own curriculum rather than borrowing one from elsewhere. The design-based research method, and the pairing of game analytics with qualitative evaluation, offer a template for the co-design workshops and classroom observation already planned at Wits.

Valakas, G., Sideri, D. and Modis, K., J, volume 8, article 38, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: Forty-nine engineering students played a workplace game for four weeks and their empathy scores rose
entry.summary:
Three researchers, two of them at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, tested a serious game called HR Toxic Workplace with 49 engineering project management students at a Malaysian public university. The students played in weekly sessions across four weeks, and empathy was measured before and after with Davis's Interpersonal Reactivity Index, which covers perspective taking, empathic concern, personal distress and fantasy. The study reports significant improvements in empathy, strongest in perspective taking and personal distress, and collected qualitative data alongside the scores.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks what teaching and assessment beyond the exam can reach, and this is a worked example of a game measuring something an exam cannot: a published instrument, a four-week schedule and a cohort of 49, all small enough to run inside a single metallurgical engineering course.

Techanamurthy, U., Chuah, K.-M. and Yee, I., Australasian Journal of Engineering Education, volume 30, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A Trivial-Pursuit-style board game for antennas and propagation is linked to higher exam grades over three years at a Madrid university
entry.summary:
Two lecturers at Universidad San Pablo-CEU and Universidad Autonoma de Madrid built a Trivial-Pursuit-style board game with 270 custom question cards and wildcards for the undergraduate 'Radiocommunications' course, commonly known elsewhere as Antennas and Propagation, and ran it once each December from 2023 to 2025. Comparing 47 students who played against 13 who did not, a Welch's t-test found players averaged 5.35 out of 10 against 2.85 for non-players (p = 0.0016, Cohen's d = 1.05), and an anonymous eleven-item survey rated the activity above 4.2 out of 5 on every question.

Why it matters here: The paper supplies a ready-made template, a question-card board game keyed to course syllabus units and run once a semester before exams, plus a rare quantitative grade comparison using Welch's t-test and Cohen's d that the Wits AHEAD project could adapt for its own crystallography or phase-transformation board game.

Domenech, A.S. and Alex-Amor, A., arXiv preprint, 2026 · Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, open access via arXiv

entry.title: Eleven experts set out how digital escape games should be designed for STEM courses, engineering education included
entry.summary:
Two researchers at the University of Education Karlsruhe and Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences interviewed eleven experts, including educators, students, software engineers and industry professionals, on how digital escape games should be designed for STEM university courses. Qualitative content analysis found that game design must follow the learning objectives, with storytelling, varied puzzles, rising difficulty and immediate feedback as essential elements, while timers, competition and rewards divided expert opinion. One of the studies the authors reviewed had already tested a digital escape game in engineering education with 31 students.

Why it matters here: Escape rooms are named directly in the project's own search brief, and this study offers concrete design guidance, on feedback, puzzle progression and the risks of timers and competition, that could shape an escape-room-style assessment activity built around crystallography or phase transformations.

Gruber, M. and Fassbender, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A three-year study of a Mexican logistics-engineering game platform links it to stronger self-directed learning skills
entry.summary:
Researchers at Tecnologico de Monterrey and Aston University deployed LOST, a serious-game platform, in an undergraduate logistics engineering course in Mexico and tracked students' self-directed learning with an adapted Fisher, King and Tague scale across academic terms from 2017 to 2020. They report significant gains across five self-directed learning factors, including self-management, openness to learning opportunities and initiative and independence in learning, alongside a supporting review of 34 Scopus-indexed studies on game-based learning in complex scenarios.

Why it matters here: This three-year, Latin American study shows how a validated self-directed learning scale can be layered onto a gamified engineering course to track effects beyond exam grades, a method the Wits AHEAD project's own surveys, interviews and classroom observation could borrow when evaluating its board-game and digital-game interventions.

Pacheco-Velazquez, E., Rodes, V. and Salinas-Navarro, D., Journal of Technology and Science Education, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Twenty-two studies, one large effect: a Ghanaian meta-analysis of gamification in higher education finds engineering among the disciplines that gain most
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Cape Coast pooled 22 independent studies of gamification in higher education in a random-effects meta-analysis. They report a large overall effect on learning outcomes (Cohen's d = 1.12, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.83) with very high heterogeneity (I squared = 98.84%). Moderator analyses found larger effects in business, mathematics and engineering, in face-to-face settings, over moderate durations of three to six months, and where the design followed a structured framework such as the Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics model; competitive designs outperformed narrative ones, and deep learning and academic performance gained more than engagement.

Why it matters here: An African synthesis the Wits study can cite for its rationale and design: it argues for a structured game design, a semester-length intervention and outcome measures that go beyond engagement, and its finding that engineering shows larger effects gives the metallurgy classroom a benchmark to test against.

Gyedu, Partey, Boafo and Agbo, Sage Open, volume 16, issue 1, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC)

entry.title: Crystal Vision: a virtual-reality game for crystallography lifts quiz scores by 9% and cuts completion time by 19% for 84 undergraduates
entry.summary:
A team spanning civil, electrical and computer engineering, information sciences and computer science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built Crystal Vision, a virtual-reality game that teaches basic crystallographic concepts to undergraduates. Systematic testing with 84 students showed a 9% rise in quiz scores (from 7.45 to 8.12 out of 10) and a 19% fall in quiz completion time (from 7.39 to 5.98 minutes) after the VR intervention. Students who felt comfortable moving through the game agreed more strongly with most survey statements, which the authors read as evidence that user comfort inside a VR game shapes learning outcomes.

Why it matters here: The closest published match to the Wits study's content: crystal structures are exactly the spatial concepts the metallurgy cohort struggles with, and this paper offers a pre-test and post-test design with timed quizzes and a comfort measure that the project could adapt for its digital game arm.

Bejjarapu, Chen, Xu, Shaffer and Garg, Journal of Chemical Education, volume 101, issue 3, pages 973 to 983, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (American Chemical Society)

entry.title: Escape our Lab: a materials-science and crystallography escape room built inside a real teaching laboratory, with the puzzle sheets published
entry.summary:
The Institute of Materials Science at TU Bergakademie Freiberg turned part of a laboratory and an adjoining seminar room into an escape room on materials science and crystallography, first run in 2019 as part of a campaign to attract students to the field. Fourteen puzzles across four rooms use real equipment such as furnaces, hardness testers, single-crystal diffraction patterns and an overhead projector, in a 60-minute short variant or a 90-minute long one; the set-up takes about an hour and the laboratory can be restored for regular teaching. The paper reports that more than 50 groups, mainly secondary pupils but also undergraduates and teachers, had played, that every puzzle can be solved without the game master's help, and that a debriefing linking each puzzle to the science is the most important step; the to-do list, hints and participation certificate are published as supporting information.

Why it matters here: A ready-made template for a low-cost, analogue game in the Wits metallurgy laboratories: the puzzles already cover diffraction and hardness, the materials are open, and the authors' observations on team dynamics and debriefing are useful design notes for the project's co-design workshops.

Schimpf, Lachmann, Wetzel, Fischer, Leineweber and Rafaja, Journal of Applied Crystallography, volume 56, pages 1544 to 1556, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY), with supporting information

entry.title: An Edge-AI gamification framework claims a 51% engagement gain in engineering classrooms
entry.summary:
Researchers at Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Punjab, and Graphic Era Deemed to be University proposed an Edge-AI gamification framework that pairs edge computing with an "Edge-AI Gamification Optimizer" algorithm to deliver real-time, personalised educational games, quizzes and competitive learning tools in engineering courses. Comparing the framework against traditional teaching, the authors report a rise of nearly 51% in student engagement, 30.7% in performance and a fall of 57% in cognitive load, alongside gains in knowledge retention, collaborative learning and motivation.

Why it matters here: The clearest fit yet for the "AI-mediated" half of this project's brief: a framework built specifically to personalise gamification in real time using AI, for the Wits team to weigh against its own plans for AI-generated or AI-mediated games, though the size of the reported gains argues for reading the framework, not yet an independent replication, with appropriate caution.

Singh and Singh, Computer Applications in Engineering Education (2025) · Peer-reviewed journal article; large reported effect sizes not yet independently replicated

entry.title: Kahoot versus paper: a controlled quiz comparison in a mechanics course at Pakistan's National University of Sciences and Technology
entry.summary:
At the School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, National University of Sciences and Technology, Islamabad, 64 engineering students volunteered for a controlled comparison of the Kahoot quiz app against paper-based quizzes across mechanics units on buckling and beam deflection, 32 students to a group. Each unit opened with a Kahoot warm-up and closed with a unit quiz; Likert-scale surveys and z-tests and t-tests found motivation, engagement, fun, concentration and learning outcomes were all significantly higher in the Kahoot group than the paper-based group.

Why it matters here: A controlled, same-topic comparison (game app against paper) rather than the single-arm surveys most gamification cases in this feed report; useful evidence for the CheMet team's own comparison of gamified and non-gamified sections, and confirmation that even a low-cost quiz app, not a bespoke game, produces a measurable gap.

Lashari, Fiayaz, Lashari, Khan, Sultana and Afzal, Computer Applications in Engineering Education 32(2), 2024 (published online 2023) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: A vector-operations video game built in Unity lifts marks in a first-year engineering science course
entry.summary:
Universidad de Ibagué's GESE research group built a Unity video game to teach vector addition, the dot product and the cross product to first-year engineering students in a basic sciences course. Forty of the roughly 100 students on the course played the game across a semester; a quantitative, non-experimental evaluation compared conceptual test scores before and after play and found an attitudinal improvement towards the course and a significant rise in academic performance, with final marks of 56.53% at 3.0 to 3.99, 39.13% at 4.0 or above and 4.34% failing.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable case to the CheMet study: a purpose-built video game replacing lecture drill for a foundational, formula-heavy topic, evaluated with the same before-and-after design the Wits team is running on crystallography and phase transformations, and a reminder that a small in-house build, not a commercial engine, can move marks.

Martínez Villalobos and Ríos Herrera, Estudios Pedagógicos 45(3), 115-125 (2019), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: The Multi-Material Marbles Game: measuring real marbles to build an Ashby chart, open source for any classroom
entry.summary:
Students measure mechanical loss coefficient, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity and density on marbles made from different material families, then plot their own Material Property Chart and reason about materials selection. Pilot studies report high engagement and increased interest in materials science; the CAD files, rules, material cards and equipment list are open source.

Why it matters here: A tactile route into structure-property relationships, the very topic the Wits study names as a learning barrier, and a ready-made open-source kit the CheMet team could trial alongside its own games.

Barnsdale, Daugela, Galos, Hülse, Tyler and Yu, 2025 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition, Montreal; DOI 10.18260/1-2--56982 · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education

entry.title: Students write the questions, the faculty prints the board: a materials-science board game across three engineering degrees
entry.summary:
A Party-and-Co style board game, its hexagonal board drawn from the graphene lattice, was built from more than 90 tests per category written by first-year mechanical engineering students and reviewed by staff, then played in Materials Science and Engineering (94 students), Microstructure and Phase Transformations (60) and Optical and Magnetic Behaviour of Materials (60). Between 80% and 84% of students said the game helped them understand the course, and 62% to 81% that they retained more than with their usual methods; participation ran at 80% to 86%.

Why it matters here: Closest published cousin of the CheMet study: a board game on phase transformations and microstructure, in the language of the students, with the survey-based evaluation the Wits team also plans. The students-as-authors step is worth borrowing for the co-design workshops.

Riquelme, de Prado, Bonache, Rams, Sánchez, Torres, Escalera Rodriguez, Rodrigo and Muñoz, Education Sciences 14(10), 1054 (2024), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo: a gamified first-year materials course for more than 1,200 learners
entry.summary:
Two adapted board games, Materials Battleships and Materials Taboo, plus custom virtual emulators of material behaviour were run for over 1,200 first-year engineering learners in person and online. Surveys reported that gamification stimulated interest in materials science and the motivation to take part, with more students saying they would pursue materials courses later.

Why it matters here: Scale evidence for the Wits study: the same mix of table games and digital play the CheMet project proposes, tested on a large first-year cohort where retention of foundational concepts is the problem.

Earle, DiCecco, Binkley, Arshad, Lucentini, Tembrevilla and Yu, 2023 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper, American Society for Engineering Education
